title: Supporting students’ conceptual development of light refraction by simulation-based open inquiry with dual-situated learning model
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a simulation-based open inquiry approach embedded in a dual-situated learning model (DSLM) can improve students’ conceptual understanding of light refraction. The authors focus on a well-known science learning problem: secondary students often hold alternative conceptions about light, especially refraction, and traditional transmission teaching has not been effective in correcting them.

The intervention combined open-inquiry science activities with the PhET Bending Light simulation and DSLM-designed learning events. Students were guided through open-ended questioning, hypothesis generation, experiment design, data analysis, class discussion, and conclusion building, while also encountering carefully designed situations intended to create cognitive dissonance and support conceptual change. The study used a concurrent mixed-methods approach, combining a one-group pretest-posttest-retention quasi-experimental design with phenomenological/discourse analysis.

Participants were 40 eleventh-grade students in a public school in northeastern Thailand. Quantitative analysis showed significant gains in conceptual understanding from pretest to posttest and retention test, with some decline at retention but performance remaining above pretest levels. Qualitative analysis suggested that students progressed through conceptual change processes such as differentiation, class extension, and reconceptualization. The authors conclude that simulation-based open inquiry within DSLM can support meaningful science learning and help students reconstruct their ideas about light refraction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-group quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with qualitative discourse analysis and no control group, so causal credibility is limited. The paper is peer-reviewed and uses pre/post/retention measures, but it does not meet stronger design criteria for green or blue evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports clear positive gains in a priority K-12 science outcome, but the evidence is from a small, non-comparative sample (n=40) and lacks an effect size. The impact appears promising but remains modest/unclear for broader generalization.

interventions.use_case: simulation-based open inquiry using the PhET Bending Light simulation to support conceptual change and inquiry learning about light refraction, Snell’s law, and total internal reflection in 11th-grade physics

finding.finding_summary: Students in the simulation-based open inquiry with DSLM showed significantly improved conceptual understanding of light refraction from pretest to posttest and retention (Friedman chi-square=44.00, p<0.01; n=40). Mean scores increased from 5.05 pretest to 11.80 posttest and remained above baseline at 10.50 on retention, indicating substantial gains in science concept understanding after the intervention.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual understanding test on light refraction (pretest, posttest, retention) scored with content-analysis rubric
finding.std_deviation: pre SD=3.02; post SD=2.84; retention SD=2.95

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative discourse analysis indicated improved conceptual change processes, including differentiation, as students used simulation evidence to revise prior ideas and construct more scientific explanations. The paper reports that the intervention supported students’ cognitive mechanism of conceptual change and more meaningful learning, though no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse / conceptual change categories (differentiation, class extension, reconceptualization)
